title: Nvidia board unanimously reinstates Jensen Huang as CEO after US government input
subtitle: Eleven days after his resignation, the board voted to bring Huang back as president, CEO, and director — a reversal the chair publicly ruled out six days earlier. Shares rose more than 30%.
author: AESOP AI Engine
body: Nvidia announced on Monday, November 23, that its board voted unanimously to reinstate Jensen Huang as president, chief executive officer, and board director, effective immediately. CFO Colette Kress, who had served as interim CEO since Huang's resignation on November 13, returns to her prior role. Board chair Harvey Jones — who publicly said six days earlier that the company did not intend to reinstate Huang — kept his seat. Nvidia shares rose more than 30% on the news.

The company's press release said the board received 'input from senior levels of the United States government' and that the input left it 'satisfied with respect to Mr. Huang's candor and ability to lead NVIDIA.' President Trump publicly took credit for the reversal. Nvidia said the independent investigation into the extramarital-affair allegations that triggered the original resignation will continue, and that the company will cooperate with ongoing government inquiries.

The sequence is extraordinary even by 2026 standards — a founder-CEO ousted after a board-led misconduct probe, an eleven-day interim regime under Kress, then a unanimous reversal after direct White House intervention. Critics have already questioned whether the board was independent enough to make that call. Separate questions remain about Huang's personal investments in AI startups that then bought Nvidia chips, the same pattern that triggered the SEC's October accounting probe into Nvidia's Singapore revenue.

A note for learners: a company's governance structure tells you how it will handle a crisis, not just how it writes the quarterly report. When a board reverses itself in less than two weeks after government pressure, that is the governance system — not an exception to it. If you ever evaluate a public company's risk profile, read the proxy and look at who can actually hold the CEO accountable. In this case the answer turned out to be 'no one, without Washington's permission.'
